entries.title: Senegal deny Morocco’s allegations of ‘contact’ with CAS amid AFCON row
entries.summary: The Court of Arbitration for Sport ruled that Senegal were the rightful winners of the 2025 African Cup of Nations.
entries.content:
The Court of Arbitration for Sport ruled that Senegal were the rightful winners of the 2025 African Cup of Nations.

The president of the Senegalese Football Federation (FSF), Abdoulaye Fall, has denied Moroccan allegations that he had “contact” with a Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) arbitrator who ruled that Senegal were the rightful winners of the 2025 African Cup of Nations.

The Moroccan federation (FRMF) alleged after Tuesday’s ruling there had been “contact” between Fall and German arbitrator Ulrich Haas, one of the three CAS panel members, 48 hours before they decided “unanimously” to award the trophy to Senegal.

“That is absolutely false. I have never had any exchange with any member of CAS,” said Fall on private television channel TFM on Wednesday.

“It surprised and astonished me that such accusations could even be made. I have never been in contact with anyone in connection with this procedure.”

In January, Senegal won a chaotic final 1-0 after extra-time.

But two months later, the Confederation of African Football (CAF) sensationally overturned the result, awarding Morocco a 3-0 victory, and the title, after many Senegalese players walked off the pitch in protest at a penalty given to the hosts with the game still goalless.

The CAF Appeals Committee had justified its decision to overturn the result and declare Morocco champions based on Articles 82 and 84 of the AFCON Regulations.

Those state that if a team “refuses to play or leaves the ground before the regular end of the match without the authorisation of the referee, it shall be considered [loser] and shall be eliminated for good from the current competition”.

However, the Senegal players eventually returned to the pitch and the final carried on.

The three-person CAS panel therefore considered the referee’s decision to restart the final showed “the conditions for resuming the match had been met”, and that articles 82 and 84 were therefore “not applicable in this case”.

The Moroccan federation has the option of lodging an appeal with the Swiss Federal Supreme Court, which does not rule on the merits of the case, but intervenes in procedural matters.

entries.title: South Africa court repeals ‘farmgate’ impeachment threat against Ramaphosa
entries.summary: The ruling hands the president ​a political reprieve by removing a finding that had exposed him to possible impeachment.
entries.content:
The ruling hands the president ​a political reprieve by removing a finding that had exposed him to possible impeachment.

South African President Cyril Ramaphosa has won a court bid challenging an independent panel’s report that had paved the way for his possible impeachment over misconduct allegations linked to a burglary-turned-political scandal called “Farmgate”.

The Western Cape High Court on Wednesday declared unlawful the 2022 findings of an independent parliamentary panel that accused Ramaphosa of a conflict of interest over the origin of large amounts of cash stolen from a sofa at his ranch in 2020.

The ruling hands Ramaphosa a political reprieve by removing a finding that had exposed him to possible impeachment at a vulnerable moment for him and his African National Congress (ANC) party.

“The court found that the panel fundamentally misconstrued its functions,” Judge Nolwazi Mabindla-Boqwana said, reading the court’s unanimous decision.

“The ‌panel went beyond its lawful remit, asked itself wrong questions and made several material errors of law.”

Ramaphosa “notes” and “will study” the court’s judgement relating to his Phala Phala game farm, the president’s office said in a statement.

“In seeking the judicial review, President Ramaphosa exercised a constitutional right,” the statement read. “In line with his respect for the rule of law including judicial independence, President Ramaphosa will study the decision of the court.”

The theft came to light after a former intelligence boss reported to the police that Ramaphosa had allegedly sought to cover up a theft of millions of US dollars in cash at his farm, initially claiming it was about $4m.

Ramaphosa has always denied wrongdoing and said the $580,000 stolen at his farm ⁠was money from the sale of buffaloes.

But the episode raised questions about ⁠why he had so much cash stuffed in furniture.

The 2022 report said the president failed to report the theft through proper channels, violated the constitution regarding paid work from his farm and directed presidential security to do police work.

The African Transformation Movement party, which is in favour of Ramaphosa’s impeachment, criticised the ruling.

Embarrassing saga

The matter has been embarrassing for a ⁠leader who came to power promising to fight corruption and clean up the image of the former liberation movement.

The ANC won about 31 percent of the vote in this month’s local elections, its worst-ever such result, extending a decline that saw it lose its national parliamentary majority in 2024 for the first time since the end of apartheid and beginning of democracy.

The Constitutional Court revived impeachment proceedings against the president in ⁠May.

It found that a 2022 parliamentary vote to stop the process ⁠was invalid and parliament should set up an impeachment inquiry.

The Western Cape High Court in July temporarily halted the inquiry pending the outcome of Wednesday’s ruling.

Ramaphosa, 74, has been head of state since 2018, and his second presidential ‌term ‌is to end in 2029. The ANC is due to elect its next leader next year when Ramaphosa will step down after two five-year terms as party leader.

entries.title: Kilmar Abrego Garcia, wrongfully deported from US, arrives in Spain
entries.summary: The Salvadoran national's lawyer said in a statement that it was 'a temporary departure'.
entries.content:
The Salvadoran national’s lawyer said in a statement that it was ‘a temporary departure’.

Kilmar Abrego Garcia relieved to not be arrested after US court hearing

Kilmar Abrego Garcia, a Salvadoran national whose wrongful deportation to El ⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠Salvador drew sharp criticism of United States President Donald Trump’s immigration crackdown, has arrived in Spain.

Abrego Garcia did not speak to reporters as he arrived at Madrid’s main international airport on Wednesday, but raised a fist as he climbed into a van.

He voluntarily departed the US a day earlier after months of legal opposition to a second deportation, this time to one of various African countries proposed by Department of Homeland Security (DHS) officials. A judge had told him to self-deport by Tuesday, The Associated Press news agency reported, citing a source familiar with the matter.

In a post on X, the DHS said: “It’s not surprising this criminal illegal alien would choose to go to Spain, a country that earlier this year was invaded by tens of thousands of illegal aliens … Good riddance.”

Abrego Garcia’s lawyer, Simon Sandoval-Moshenberg, described the move as “a temporary departure”.

“Mr Abrego Garcia has many options to return to the United States as the husband of a US citizen spouse and the father of a US citizen child. We don’t expect that to happen under this administration,” he said in a statement.

Sandoval-Moshenberg noted the US government had sought to deport Garcia “in shackles on an ICE Air flight to Liberia”.

US Senator Chris Van Hollen, a Democrat from Maryland, the state where Abrego Garcia ⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠lived with his family for around a decade before being deported, said the Trump administration “was forced to come to this agreement that respects Kilmar’s will.”

The departure of Abrego Garcia, 31, brings an end to a legal fight that, at one point, reached the US ⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠Supreme Court.

US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) arrested Abrego Garcia in Baltimore in March 2025. He was then transferred to a megaprison in El Salvador despite a prior court order barring him from being sent to the country because of the risk of persecution.

A US official later called the transfer an “administrative error”.

After the Supreme Court ordered the government to facilitate Garcia’s return, prosecutors secured a criminal indictment charging him with human smuggling in a case stemming from an earlier incident. The Trump administration then brought him back ⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠to the US in June 2025. It later tried to deport him to Liberia ⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠after a US judge dismissed the human smuggling charge.

entries.title: US Army detonates toxic lead explosives in Iowa amid health concerns
entries.summary: The US Army destroys nearly 4,500kg of lead azide amid fears of toxic fallout affecting residents, farms and livestock.
entries.content:
The US Army destroys nearly 4,500kg of lead azide amid fears of toxic fallout affecting residents, farms and livestock.

Five tonnes of explosives set to blow up in Iowa

A large stockpile of lead-rich explosives in the Midwestern state of Iowa has been destroyed in controlled detonations by the United States Army, ending a brief legal battle spurred by concerns that toxic dust from the fallout would endanger residents, livestock and farmland.

Video showed that the nearly 4,500kg (10,000lb) of lead azide – a highly volatile, lead-based explosive that has been used in military munitions since World War I – was detonated in two successive open-air detonations on Wednesday at around 9am (15:00 GMT).

Environmental groups have raised concerns that the explosions would release particles that could eventually land on homes, crops and livestock far beyond the detonation site, potentially travelling more than 160km (100 miles).

Before the detonations at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant, outgoing Republican Governor Kim Reynolds declared a disaster emergency across three counties in southeastern Iowa – Des Moines, Lee and Van Buren – activating state and county emergency response plans.

Shortly before the controlled detonations, Assistant Secretary of the Army Jordan Gillis appeared in a video on X, discussing the decision behind the detonation and explaining how the Army is attempting to mitigate the particles released. “The choice that we faced here was between a spontaneous, uncontrolled detonation of dangerous material or a controlled detonation where we could choose the time and place to optimize the conditions to deliver the best result – not just for our operation but for the safety of the public,” Gillis said.

Revised wind projections released by the Army on Tuesday showed that airborne lead particles would shift southwest into northeast Missouri, prompting health officials there to advise residents 8km to 32km (5 to 20 miles) southwest of the plant to shelter indoors with windows and doors shut until an all-clear is issued.

A looming hazard for communities under strain

Amid a groundswell of concern over the prospect of toxic lead fallout, some residents have warned of the added burden the operation could place on communities already contending with chronic economic pressures, including a shortage of affordable housing, rising food costs and stretched local services.

The detonation’s impact will be felt across Des Moines County, which covers the city of Burlington and the rural community of Middletown, immediately adjacent to the ammunition plant.

Home to about 38,000 Iowans, the county had 38 percent of its households below the Asset Limited, Income Constrained, Employed (ALICE) threshold in 2024, according to the latest figures published by United for ALICE, a national research initiative.

“We shouldn’t have to experience an environmental disaster to become worthy of national attention or investment,” Megan Brincks, chairwoman of the Burlington Homelessness Task Force, told Al Jazeera.

Brincks, a Burlington resident who previously worked in the ammunition plant’s chemistry laboratory, stressed that the Army’s shelter-in-place orders cannot suspend the daily obligations of those whose work keeps the community running.

“Our food-insecure families will still need food tomorrow,” Brincks said, adding: “People experiencing homelessness will still need shelter. Individuals will still need transportation to medical appointments.”

“Unfortunately, the world doesn’t stop spinning because this is happening in our back yard.”

‘Land is their currency’

The blasts rocked one of southeastern Iowa’s most heavily cultivated stretches of land in a state that ranks second only to California in agricultural output value.

According to the US Department of Agriculture (USDA), Iowa is a leading producer of corn and soya beans and ranks first in the country in commercial red meat and egg production.

Across Des Moines County, about 648 farms span nearly 60,300 hectares (149,000 acres), including more than 49,775 hectares (123,000 acres) of cropland.

On Tuesday, Richard Fordyce, an undersecretary at the USDA, said the agency and the Iowa Department of Agriculture and Land Stewardship estimated that about 350 farms across Iowa and Missouri could lie within the projected plume area.

The prospect has stoked alarm over the risk of lead leaching into soil and groundwater, compromising crops and livestock and jeopardising the livelihoods of the farmers whose land underpins a vital part of the country’s food supply.

Will Sander, an associate professor of preventive medicine and public health at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, said much of Iowa’s corn and soya bean harvest has already been completed, reducing the likelihood of acute exposure to this season’s crops.

Cattle producers, he said, should cover feed and water supplies where possible to limit animals’ ingestion of lead dust even if they cannot bring their herds under shelter.

“The acute exposure is the biggest risk in this situation, … that lead will not have dispersed and diluted into the environment,” Sander told Al Jazeera.

“For [these] farmers, land is their currency,” Eri Saikawa, a professor of environmental sciences at Emory University, said. “It is not acceptable that their livelihood is impacted this way. It also impacts all of us who rely on these farmers and their crops.”

entries.title: Trump announces new trade tariffs: Which countries are affected?
entries.summary: The US is planning tariffs on 14 economies it accuses of using subsidies to help their industries overproduce.
entries.content:
The US is aiming tariffs at 14 economies it accuses of using subsidies to help their factories overproduce.

The Trump administration has announced plans to impose new trade tariffs on 14 of its major trading partners, including China, the European Union and India, accusing them of flooding world markets with cheap goods. China faces the highest rates.

The Office of the US Trade Representative (USTR) announced the duties on Wednesday following an eight-month investigation into what Washington calls “structural excess capacity”.

A senior US official told Reuters that USTR defines this as countries “promoting production and capacity divorced from the realities of demand and market principles”, including through subsidies and other industrial policies.

The tariffs are the latest attempt to rebuild Trump’s sweeping import taxes that the US Supreme Court struck down in February.

Here is what we know so far.

What new tariffs are being announced?

The latest tariffs are being imposed under Section 301, part of a 1974 US trade law, which allows Washington to penalise countries it determines are treating US businesses unfairly. Trump used it to place large tariffs on Chinese goods during his first term, and those tariffs survived challenges in court.

The new tariffs are Trump’s latest attempt to bring back the “Liberation Day” tariffs he announced in April 2025 shortly after he began his second term in the White House. He imposed those under an emergency powers law but, in February this year, the Supreme Court ruled that the law did not allow him to impose trade tariffs.

“It’s supposed to be for international economic emergencies,” Dmitry Grozoubinski, a trade policy expert, said of the emergency law. “Tariffs are like taxes. You can’t really fight emergencies with mild taxes.”

The administration then used another law to put temporary 10 percent tariffs on trading partners in place, which ran out in July. It then replaced those with tariffs of 10 to 12.5 percent on 60 economies, which together supply almost everything the US imports. This time it used Section 301, arguing that those countries do not do enough to keep out goods made with forced labour.

Grozoubinski said Section 301 was designed to allow a president to hit back quickly at one country over one industry, not to tax almost every import. “The legislation is supposed to be a scalpel, and they used it like a flamethrower,” he said. “It is not meant to set the US tariff code, which is what this effectively did.”

The recent investigation into the “structural excess capacity” of trading partners began in March and covered industries from steel and cars to computer chips and solar panels. It examined government subsidies, wages suppressed by the state and the operations of state-owned companies.

Washington argues that this support enables foreign factories to sell their goods more cheaply around the world, undercutting American manufacturers and discouraging investment in the US. The senior official told Reuters that the new duties would not be added on top of the forced labour tariffs.

Which countries have been targeted

The investigation covered 16 economies, and tariffs have been proposed for 14 of them: China, Bangladesh, Cambodia, the European Union, India, Indonesia, Japan, South Korea, Malaysia, Singapore, Switzerland, Taiwan, Thailand and Vietnam. For now, Mexico and Norway, which were also investigated, have been spared.

The Trump administration views China as the biggest offender, pointing to its steel, aluminium, electric cars, household appliances and solar panels industries. Beijing rejects the accusation and says its exports are simply competitive. Washington also accuses Chinese companies of investing in Vietnam, Indonesia and Cambodia to bypass earlier US tariffs.

For the other economies, Washington pointed to the large trade surpluses of Germany and Ireland as evidence against the EU. It also singled out the car industries of China and Japan, Singapore’s computer chips and Norway’s fuel and seafood exports for criticism.

What will the new tariff rates be?

The senior official cited by Reuters did not provide rates for most countries ahead of their publication in the Federal Register. However, China will face the highest charges. The official said its proposed 20 percent excess capacity tariff would come on top of the roughly 25 percent in tariffs set during Trump’s first term. That keeps China above Vietnam, which also faces a proposed rate of 20 percent.

The official said the new duties would not break the tariff limits in trade deals the Trump administration has negotiated. According to earlier Reuters reporting, those include caps of 15 percent for the EU, Japan and South Korea, and 19 percent for Malaysia.

For China, the limit is 20 percent on tariffs imposed during Trump’s second term, under a trade truce with Beijing that expires on January 10.

India has no signed trade deal with the US. The two sides agreed the outline of one in February, but it was never finalised, and talks have dragged on for months. On November 14, Indian foreign minister S Jaishankar said a deal could be sealed soon.

Why is Trump doing this now?

Grozoubinski said the timing is significant. The proposal comes just weeks after midterm elections in which Trump’s Republican Party suffered unprecedented electoral losses, in which the cost of living and trade tariffs were major issues. A Reuters/Ipsos poll after the vote indicated that 62 percent of respondents would support efforts to scrap trade tariffs.

“One interpretation is, like, OK, they’re going to chill out on these tariffs, because basically every time they say the word tariffs, people remember that their costs are really high and get angrier,” Grozoubinski said. “This shows that at least on some level, they are still prepared despite the headwinds, to go ahead and push that button.”

Hisham Wahby, an independent political analyst, said the key question after the vote was whether Trump would “double down or pull back”. Days after the midterms, Trump named his longtime adviser, the hardline anti-immigration activist Stephen Miller, as White House chief of staff. Wahby said that “was a clear indicator he is going to double down”.

US importers are currently challenging the forced labour tariffs at the US Court of International Trade, and Grozoubinski called the reasoning behind them “incredibly dubious”. Accusations about subsidies, he said, will be easier to defend.

“One theory is maybe they’re going to impose these little tariffs now, but if their big tariffs on everybody on forced labour get cancelled, they can fall back and say, we’ve already done the investigation,” he said. In that case, he added, the new tariffs would “replace the tariffs that replaced the tariffs that replaced the tariffs that replaced the Liberation Day tariffs”.

The announcement also comes weeks before the US-China trade truce, agreed between President Donald Trump and China’s President Xi Jingping last year, runs out, while trade talks with India remain unfinished.

Wahby said the decision is hard to explain in economic terms. “He lost the midterms because of the cost of living, because of the price of goods. Small businesses were suffering,” he said. “Households are suffering, small businesses are suffering, and you double down on it.”

Could the new tariffs be struck down?

Grozoubinski said the new tariffs will certainly be challenged in court. However, he said they were likely to stay in place while the cases went on, because lower court rulings are usually appealed and put on hold. The emergency tariffs, he noted, stayed in force for months after the trade court first ruled against them, until the Supreme Court struck them down.

He added that these latest tariffs stand a better chance of surviving than earlier ones, because foreign subsidies are a more believable complaint than forced labour.

“There’s probably something there,” he said. If the investigation genuinely found unfair practices, he said, the Supreme Court may decide that Trump is within his rights and that it is up to Congress to stop him.

“Of the tariffs he has imposed so far, these, at least from the outside and without having any of the details, are probably the most legally robust,” he said.

Will Trump’s tariffs restore manufacturing in the US?

The Trump administration argues that tariffs will push companies to build factories in the US to avoid paying import duties.

Grozoubinski said tariffs could help American companies that compete with imports, but will hurt those that rely on them. A US carmaker gains when foreign cars cost more, he said, but loses when the imported steel, engines and parts it needs also cost more.

The bigger problem, he said, is that nobody knows how long the tariffs will last. A new factory can take a decade or more to pay for itself, while Trump raises and lowers tariffs as negotiations shift. Congress could also limit his power to impose them, and a future president could scrap them altogether.

A company weighing a new US factory would worry about that, he said: “I can’t guarantee those tariffs will still be around for all the 10 years I need them.”

“If I wanted to use the US tariff code to encourage people to build factories in the US, I would not do it this way,” he said.

What is the likely fallout?

The most immediate cost is likely to fall on US companies and households that depend on imports. “If you make components from somewhere else more expensive, then, really simplistically, the people who buy them in your country lose out, and the people who make them in your country win,” Grozoubinski said.

Wahby said small businesses would be among the hardest hit. “How is that going to increase jobs if small businesses can’t manage to buy what they need from China?” he asked.

Markets were already uneasy, and US stocks came under pressure on Tuesday as reports of the plan emerged.

Abroad, the tariffs risk straining the US-China truce, which expires in January, and could complicate trade talks with India. They are also likely to anger US allies who already accuse Washington of breaching existing trade agreements. “This is not a free market economy when you’re putting tariffs on everybody,” Wahby said.

At home, the move sets up a clash with Democrats, who take control of both chambers of Congress in January. Wahby said they would push back, but their power is limited because Trump can veto legislation. “They will stand up to him, but we don’t know how effectively,” he said.

entries.title: US court convicts Huawei of theft: A history of Chinese firm’s global woes
entries.summary: Chinese tech giant has faced legal problems from Europe to Asia, and its products have been banned in trade war with US.
entries.content:
Chinese tech giant has also faced legal problems from Europe to Asia while its products have been banned during trade war with the US.

A United States jury has found Chinese tech giant Huawei and three of its subsidiaries guilty of serious violations, including defrauding banks and conspiracy to steal trade secrets from US firms.

The verdict on Tuesday was handed down in a New York federal court and came after a lengthy trial of the Chinese electronics and tech giant.

Huawei faced multiple allegations, including accusations of engaging in a criminal racketeering conspiracy. But the company’s troubles extend as well to a number of other countries, including Canada and Australia.

“For over two decades, Huawei built its global empire on a foundation of fraud, theft and deception,” said Assistant Attorney General A Tysen Duva of the Criminal Division of the US Department of Justice.

“Huawei’s crimes threatened the US financial system, took advantage of American companies that compete honestly in the global telecommunications market and undermined our national security.”

Here’s what we know:

What was Huawei convicted of?

Huawei was convicted on 10 of 11 counts along with its Chinese subsidiary Huawei Device Co Ltd and US subsidiaries Futurewei Technologies Inc and Huawei Device USA Inc.

The jury found them guilty of conspiracy to steal trade secrets, conspiracy to commit wire and bank fraud, wire fraud, bank fraud, conspiracy to defraud the United States, conspiracy to violate the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA), substantive violations of IEEPA and money laundering conspiracy.

In a statement, the US Justice Department revealed specific instances of alleged misconduct.

A Huawei employee stole information about Tappy, a robot developed by T-Mobile, although both firms had signed a nondisclosure agreement, the department alleged.

In another instance, Huawei engineers were accused of copying the source code of Cisco routers.

Another employee allegedly disguised as someone else went to work for the US tech company CNEX even though the firm had earlier indicated it did not want to work directly with Huawei.

The convictions also related to allegations that Huawei operated in Iran and North Korea, countries under US sanctions, and made false statements to US officials and banks to hide that fact.

Huawei, however, was acquitted of the most serious charge: engaging in criminal racketeering conspiracy.

Criminal charges were first brought against the company in 2019. Its lawyers said investigators used isolated cases of wrongdoing by a few employees to paint a grand conspiracy.

Sentencing is set for September although Huawei’s lawyers said the company will appeal.

Huawei is expected to pay huge sums in penalties.

Is this part of the US-China tech tussle?

Yes. Washington and Beijing are in a race to command technological advancements, particularly artificial intelligence.

Beijing has condemned the verdict as an attempt by Washington aimed at “containing and suppressing” Chinese firms.

“The Chinese government firmly opposes movies by the US side aimed at containing and suppressing Chinese enterprises, and firmly supports Chinese enterprises’ lawful rights,” the Chinese Ministry of Foreign Affairs said in a statement on Wednesday.

The verdict was announced as the Nvidia scandal has been rocking Silicon Valley. Jensen Huang, the cofounder and CEO of the advanced chips company, is under US investigation for potentially leaking critical information to China after it was revealed a woman he had a romantic relationship with could have been a Chinese spy.

Beijing has denied involvement.

Nvidia’s chips power AI products, and Washington has restricted the company from selling its most advanced semiconductors to China. Nvidia is the world’s second most valuable company after only Apple with a market capitalisation of more than $4.4 trillion.

What issues does Huawei face elsewhere?

For years, the company has been blacklisted in the US, where it is restricted from selling equipment to telecommunications carriers without special approval because of security concerns.

Other US allies have flagged it over concerns that the company is too close to Chinese authorities:

  • Australia and New Zealand – joined the US in banning the firm from supplying 5G equipment and services in 2018.
  • Britain – banned telecom providers from buying new Huawei 5G equipment after 2020 and set a deadline of 2027 to remove all existing Huawei gear from networks.
  • Canada – barred Huawei from supplying equipment for 4G and 5G networks in 2022. In 2018, Canadian authorities arrested Meng Wanzhou, the chief financial officer and daughter of founder Ren Zhengfei. She was extradited to the US, where she faced allegations of misleading an HSBC banker about Huawei’s business in Iran. Charges were later dropped, and Meng returned to China in a prisoner swap.
  • Europe – In 2024, major German providers like Deutsche Telekom agreed to remove Chinese-made telecom equipment from 5G networks, including those from Huawei and ZTE, another Chinese manufacturer, before a 2029 deadline. Germany is also preparing sweeping bans on Chinese mobile network equipment that essentially could bar Huawei and ZTE. Other countries – including Estonia, Denmark, France, Italy, Latvia, Lithuania, Portugal, Romania and Sweden – have outright banned or restricted Huawei and other Chinese manufacturers.
  • Japan, Taiwan and India – have also either completely excluded or restricted the company.
